definitions: All machines use alphabet {0,1}. An omitted edge is absent; each item specifies its epsilon edges. State sets are mathematical sets. Questions concern acceptance after all input is consumed. This sheet intentionally excludes answer indices and explanations.

items.prompt: An ε-NFA reads the entire word 01. One possible path consumes both symbols and ends in an accepting state; every other possible path rejects or stops early. What is the result?
options: Reject: every path must accept.
Reject: accepting and rejecting paths cancel.
Accept: one fully consuming accepting path is enough.
Undefined: an NFA must choose exactly one path in advance.
items.transfer: Explain why counting the accepting paths is unnecessary for this accept/reject decision, and why a path that leaves input unread is insufficient.

items.prompt: The current active set is {q0,q1}. On input 1, q0 has no destination and q1 reaches q2. There are no ε-edges. What is the next active set?
options: ∅, because one branch stopped
items.transfer: Change q1 so it also has no 1-destination. What is the next active set, and can later input revive it without any active state?

items.prompt: Start at q0; only q2 accepts. There are no ε-edges. q0 on 0→{q0}, on 1→{q0,q1}; q1 on 0→{q2}, on 1→∅; q2 has no symbol destinations. Does the machine accept 101?
options: Yes, because the prefix 10 reached q2.
Yes, because q0 remains active.
No, because any branch that stops makes the whole word reject.
No: after all three symbols the active set is {q0,q1}, with no accepting state.
items.transfer: Trace the same machine on 1010. State the final active set and decision; explain how it differs from 101.

items.prompt: The only ε-edges are q0→q1, q1→q0 and q1→q2. What is the ε-closure of {q0}?
options: {q0,q1}, because a cycle prevents further search
An infinite set, because the cycle can be repeated
items.transfer: Why can a visited-state traversal stop even though there are infinitely many walks around the q0–q1 cycle?

items.prompt: A machine contains several ε-edges and an accepting state. What is the ε-closure of the empty active set ∅?
options: All states with an ε-edge.
All accepting states.
∅: no starting state exists from which to follow an edge.
The closure of the machine's original start state.
items.transfer: Contrast closure(∅) with closure({q}) when q has no outgoing ε-edge.

items.prompt: Start at q0; only q2 accepts. The only symbol edge is q0 on 0→q1, and the only ε-edge is q1→q2. After reading the word 0, which closed active set and decision are correct?
options: {q1,q2}; accept
{q1}; reject
{q2}; accept, with q1 removed because it has an ε-edge
{q0,q1,q2}; accept
items.transfer: Why must the simulator close the destinations after a symbol move? What is the result for the empty word in this machine?

items.prompt: An ε-NFA starts at q0, with ε-edges q0→q1 and q1→q2. There are no other ε-edges. What is the start state of its subset-construction DFA?
options: The single state q0.
The set of all accepting states.
∅ until the first symbol is read.
The subset {q0,q1,q2}.
items.transfer: If only q2 is accepting, does this start subset accept the empty word? Explain without consuming a symbol.

items.prompt: The NFA accepting set is {q2}. Its reachable subset DFA contains a state whose members are {q0,q2,q3}. How is that DFA state classified?
options: Rejecting, because not all members accept.
Accepting, because at least one member is q2.
Accepting only if q2 was entered without an ε-edge.
Neither accepting nor rejecting until one member is chosen.
items.transfer: Give one accepting and one rejecting subset for the same NFA accepting set. Explain why the number of rejecting members is irrelevant.

items.prompt: The subset construction reaches the empty subset ∅. What are its destinations on 0 and 1, even if the original NFA contains ε-cycles?
options: Both destinations are ∅.
Both destinations are the original start closure.
Each destination is an arbitrary accepting subset.
The transitions are undefined, so the constructed DFA cannot be complete.
items.transfer: Is ∅ necessarily reachable in every subset construction? Distinguish the full power set from the subsets reached from the start.

items.prompt: An ε-NFA has five states. What can be concluded about the number of reachable states in its subset-construction DFA?
options: Exactly five.
Exactly 32.
At most 32; some subsets may be unreachable.
Unbounded, because ε-cycles permit arbitrarily long walks.
items.transfer: Construct a five-state NFA whose only reachable subset is {q0}: specify its start, symbol moves from q0 and relevant ε-moves. What happens to the other four states?

items.prompt: Why does the full reachable subset construction recognize the same language as its ε-NFA?
options: It agrees on every word shown in a finite test panel, which proves all future words.
For every prefix, its DFA state equals the ε-NFA's closed active set; this invariant extends by each symbol and gives the same final acceptance.
It merges all states that have the same accepting flag.
It selects a single successful NFA path before reading the input.
items.transfer: State the invariant for the empty prefix and explain one inductive step. Why do agreement checks only through length eight provide tests rather than the whole proof?

items.prompt: An NFA has no ε-edges. Both q0 and q1 accept; q0 is the start, both symbol moves from q0 go to q1, and both moves from q1 loop to q1. Reachable subset construction yields {q0} and {q1}. Is this necessarily a minimal DFA?
options: Yes: reachable subset construction always minimizes.
Yes: different subset labels always mean different future languages.
No: minimization would require preserving the original two state names.
No: one accepting state looping on both symbols recognizes the same language.
items.transfer: Which language does this machine recognize, including the empty word? Separate eliminating unreachable subsets from merging equivalent reachable states.
